newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Tender disputes cloud Zimbabwe investment climate.
newsitem.headline: Tender disputes cloud Zimbabwe investment climate.

text.p: Zimbabwe's drive to win vital foreign investment for its long-suffering economy is being undermined by lack of transparency in its tender system, local political and business analysts charged on Wednesday.
But a senior government official denied the tender system was faulty or would affect investors' attitudes.

The analysts were commenting on the sacking by the government of the entire board of the state Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA) for stoutly opposing what it saw as an underhand deal with Malaysia to privatise the power utility.

"All our efforts will count for very little if the world thinks we are running a closed system. The demand internationally is for greater transparency," business consultant John Robertson said of the dismissal.

Transport and Energy Minister Simon Moyo said on Wednesday President Robert Mugabe had approved the replacement of ZESA's 10-member board which was pressing the government to rescind a letter of intent it signed last month with Malaysia power producer YTL Corp Bhd.
Moyo was unavailable for more comment, but a government official who declined to be identified said the power deal should be viewed as a private placement and anxious investors would be told so.
"We are committed to a transparent tender system but this was a private placement and we are also entitled to look for partners this way," he said, declining to discuss the issue further.

Under the deal with Malaysia, YTL would invest Z$6 billion (U.S.$580 million) in the privatisation of ZESA's Hwange Power Station in northern Zimbabwe, and control 51 percent of the equity in a joint venture company to be established for the project.
Business analysts say it is the biggest tender awarded in Zimbabwe since independence from Britain in 1980.

Solomon Tawengwa, the chairman of the sacked board, said the government had not informed ZESA of the deal which he said was a departure from an earlier government agreement to follow tender procedures.
Before the government's deal with Malaysia, ZESA had already invited bids and six foreign companies had been shortlisted, top of them a British firm, while YTL was at the bottom of the list.
"If we are going to get business and win investors' confidence, we cannnot afford to appear like under-hand players," Robertson told Reuters.

The quarrel over the ZESA project is the third highly-publicised tender dispute in the past six months in which Mugabe's government ignored tender procedures or accepted bids for multi-million dollar projects under controversial circumstances.

Earlier this year, Mugabe was forced to cancel a tender awarded to communications giants Ericsson to establish Zimbabwe's first cellular phone system following complaints by the United States and German governments the tendering system was not open.
The fresh tender was subsequently won by Siemens.

Another bid for the construction of a new international airport for Harare also raised eyebrows and public criticism after the government awarded it to a Cyprus-based firm which has links with Mugabe's nephew, Leo Mugabe, and which critics said failed to meet the tender's criteria.

Mugabe -- who has been on an investment drive around the world in the past two years -- told a Zimbabwe investment promotion conference in Hamburg, Germany, last week that his government was committed to an open tender system.

A number of Western countries are querying the Malaysia deal, and are openly asking whether it will be the model of how the Zimbabwean government -- whose privatisation programme has been on the table for years -- will proceed.
"The world is not just looking at words, but at actions," commented one Western diplomat.
Charles Rukuni, a Zimbabwean editor and publisher of a monthly political newsletter, The Insider, said the tender disputes were damaging the southern African state's investment climate.
